CHARLOTTE LATIN SCHOOL Inside Charlotte Latin College Support
SEGMENT 2 — THE ACADEMIC CASE
Rigor & Credentials
AP recognition and National Merit across three editions, a weighted transcript colleges are taught
to read, and the credential data the school doesn't publish.
Charlotte Latin makes its academic case through a rigorous, benchmark-gated Honors/AP curriculum, a
strong and partially quantified record on AP recognition and National Merit, and a transcript the school takes
care to explain to colleges. This segment reports what the school publishes — and is candid about the
credential data it does not.
AP recognition and National Merit — three editions
The school publishes AP Scholar and National Merit counts as rolling three-year aggregates in each Upper
School Profile. Reading three successive editions side by side shows the recent picture (windows overlap by
design, so these are successive published aggregates, not independent single years):

The 2020–22 and 2021–23 editions also named National Hispanic Scholars (5 and 4 respectively). AP
Scholar with Distinction is the College Board's top tier of the three (awarded for an average score of at least
3.5 across all exams taken, with 3+ on five or more), so a rising count in the newest edition reflects breadth
of strong AP performance.
Most recent single class. For the Class of 2026 specifically, the school's own October 2025 announcement
reported 12 National Merit Semifinalists and 18 Commended Students — the Commended threshold
that year corresponding to a National Merit Selection Index of 210 or higher. (Individual student names are
omitted here by design.)
AP exam pass rates are not published
The school offers AP in 23 subjects (up from 22) and requires every student in an AP class to sit the AP exam —
but it does not publish the percentage of exams scoring 3 or higher. AP Scholar counts recognize high
performers; they are not the same as a school-wide pass rate. The absence of a published pass rate is a
transparency limitation, not evidence of weak results. Families can ask the office directly for the share of exams
scoring 3+.
Standardized testing
The current profile does not publish an SAT or ACT range for its classes — consistent with the test-optional
era, in which many independent schools have stopped printing score bands. The most recent
school-published range appears in the older 2017–18 profile, which listed a middle ACT band of roughly
27–34; that figure is dated and should be read only as historical context, not a current statistic.

SAT/ACT ranges: a publication gap, with a labeled secondary figure available
Because the school does not publish current score ranges, the only score figures in circulation are self-reported
aggregations on review sites such as Niche and PrivateSchoolReview. Those are self-reported (not
school-reported) and are treated here as secondary — they sit alongside the gap, they do not close it. For a
current, authoritative range, families should request the most recent middle-50% SAT/ACT directly from the
college-counseling office.
Grading, and how it's explained to colleges
• Weighted 4-point GPA. AP and Honors courses receive one additional quality point.
• No class rank. The school does not report class rank (covered in depth in the Fit & Rank segment).
• Middle-School high-school courses appear on the transcript but are excluded from any GPA
calculation.
• Benchmark-gated rigor. Students must meet faculty benchmarks for Honors/AP placement (with a few
open-enrollment AP exceptions such as AP Psychology, AP Economics, AP Environmental Science, and
AP Computer Science Principles).
Crucially, the profile actively contextualizes the transcript for admissions readers. Its math note explains that
because the Honors track is “unusually rigorous and fast-paced, many fine math students are placed in
‘standard’ courses” — a deliberate signal to colleges not to read a standard-track placement as a lack of
ability. That kind of explanatory framing is exactly what a School Profile is for.
For students who exhaust the catalog
The model is an in-house, honors/AP-rich curriculum rather than heavy dual enrollment. Beyond the 23 AP
subjects, advanced and post-AP-style options include Honors Java Data Structures, Honors Bioengineering
and Honors Electrical Engineering, AP Cybersecurity: Networking Fundamentals, and honors history
seminars, supported by the school's Fab Lab and Innovation/Design pathway. Dual enrollment is not
emphasized in the published materials.
Segment sources: Charlotte Latin Upper School Profiles (2020–22, 2021–23, and 2023–25 editions) and the school's Oct. 2025
National Merit announcement; 2017–18 profile for the historical ACT band. Score figures on Niche/PrivateSchoolReview are
self-reported and secondary. Student names omitted throughout.

CHARLOTTE LATIN SCHOOL Inside Charlotte Latin College Support
SEGMENT 4 — APPLICATION SUPPORT
The Application Itself
A three-person essay team, review before submission, and the two money conversations kept
carefully separate.
This segment covers the machinery of the application itself — essays, letters, review, and the two distinct
money conversations (college-awarded merit versus the school's own tuition aid). Charlotte Latin's most
distinctive application-support asset is a dedicated three-person essay team layered on top of the
counselors.
Essay support: a dedicated three-person team
Three named essay specialists support seniors — Andrea Powell, Marty Minchin, and Mary Beth Foster ’99.
Minchin is a professional writer and editor who teaches college-level writing at UNC Charlotte; Foster is a
Charlotte-area writer and a Latin alumna. Support runs from optional summer essay workshops the summer
before senior year, through iterative essay review and feedback, into a senior “College Application
Bootcamp.” Having writing specialists distinct from the college counselors is an unusual amount of
dedicated essay capacity for a school this size.
Letters, and review before submission
• Counselor letters. Counselors write the school's letter of recommendation and advocate individually for
each student.
• Every application reviewed. The senior-year process explicitly includes proofreading each essay and
application prior to submission — so a second set of eyes sees an application before it goes out.
Early Decision / Early Action
ED/EA strategy is handled through senior seminars on the application process and junior-year
testing-and-timeline discussions, within the school's adherence to the NACAC principles of good practice.
The school does not publish specific ED/EA policy language; families should confirm the office's current
guidance directly.
The two money conversations — kept separate
College-awarded merit scholarships
Charlotte Latin students have historically won marquee college merit awards, including the Morehead-Cain
and Robertson Scholarships at UNC-Chapel Hill — a 2022 senior received the Morehead-Cain, which
admits a low single-digit percentage of applicants and covers the full cost of attendance.
College-merit dollar totals are not published
The school does not publish aggregate college-merit-scholarship dollars or breadth for recent classes. Named
marquee awards are documented; a class-wide total is not. This is a transparency gap on the college-merit
question specifically — ask the office for recent totals and for mid-tier merit at schools like Alabama, South
Carolina, or Miami.

The school's own tuition assistance (a different question)
Separately — and this answers “can we afford Latin?”, not “what will colleges award?” — the school
distributes over $3 million in need-based tuition assistance through the Clarity platform (roughly $3.125M in
2021–22, reaching about 14% of students), with a January 15 application deadline. This is the school's
internal aid and is entirely distinct from college-awarded merit scholarships.
Need-based aid navigation, and upperclass work
Financial-aid programming for the college process (a “Financial Aid for College” session and a Grade 12
Parent College Night) is part of the calendar. Explicit published detail on FAFSA/CSS Profile walk-throughs,
award-letter comparison and appeals, and internship or part-time-job placement for upperclassmen is limited
— these appear to be handled within seminars rather than documented as standalone services; families can
ask how hands-on that support is.

CHARLOTTE LATIN SCHOOL Inside Charlotte Latin College Support
SEGMENT 1 — THE COUNSELING ENGINE
People, Timing & Tools
Four counselors, a freshman-year start, and SCOIR-powered admissions data.
Charlotte Latin's College Counseling Office is a four-counselor operation with a long-stable core, a
dedicated essay-support team, and a counselor assigned to every student from the freshman year. This
segment lays out who staffs the office, when individualized college work begins, and the concrete data tools
families can use.
Who staffs the office
The 2025–26 Upper School Profile lists the office as four full-time counselors, a registrar, an administrative
assistant, and three essay specialists. The counseling roles are held by:
Role Named staff
Director of College Counseling Jody Jennings
Associate Directors (3) Haley Cripps · Lucy Smith · Alex Segura
Registrar Sonja Turpin
Essay specialists (3) Andrea Powell · Marty Minchin · Mary Beth Foster ’99
Administrative assistant Stacey Rommich
Counselor-to-student load. With a 2025–26 senior class of about 145 and Upper School enrollment of
roughly 586 across grades 9–12, four counselors work out to approximately 36–37 seniors per counselor at
the point of most intensive application work, and roughly 145 Upper School students per counselor when
spread across all four grades. The three essay specialists sit on top of that ratio as added senior-year
capacity.
When individualized work begins
Every student is assigned a college counselor in the freshman year — language the school has used
consistently since at least its 2017–18 profile — so the counselor relationship is built over four years rather
than compressed into junior and senior year. Grade 9 programming opens with college-counseling seminars
and student registration in SCOIR, the office's data platform; grade-appropriate seminars then run every
year through senior spring (self-discovery and interest-mapping in the underclass years; testing timelines,
essays, interviews, and the application mechanics later).
Staff stability
The office grew from three counselors in 2017–18 to four by roughly 2019, and the four-counselor core —
Jennings, Cripps, Smith, and Segura — appears consistently across the 2022–23, 2023–24, and 2025–26
profiles. That multi-year continuity is a genuine strength for families, since the same counselor is likely to
carry a student from assignment through graduation. Support-role titles (registrar and administrative
assistant) have seen some turnover across editions.

Counselor backgrounds
Backgrounds across the team lean toward secondary-school college counseling and higher education rather
than the admissions-office side of the desk:
• Jody Jennings (Director) — B.A. from Wofford College; has served on the University of Tampa
counselor advisory board; long-tenured, listed as director as far back as the 2017–18 profile.
• Haley Cripps (Associate Director) — higher-education background with study at Vanderbilt University;
previously an educational consultant with EWC Consulting.
• Lucy Smith (Associate Director) — M.Ed. in School Counseling from UNC-Chapel Hill and a B.A. from
the University of Maryland; prior school-counseling roles, plus service on admissions advisory boards for
Ohio State and the University of Pittsburgh and NACAC/SACAC college-fair planning.
• Alex Segura (Associate Director) — role confirmed as Associate Director of College Counseling;
individual public professional detail is limited.
On the “former admissions officer” question
None of the four counselors is documented in public sources as a former college-admissions officer. That is a
factual description of the team's career path — school counseling and higher education rather than the
admissions office — not a mark against the office's effectiveness. Advisory-board service (Tampa, Ohio State,
Pittsburgh) does reflect ongoing working relationships with admissions offices.
The data tools families get
Charlotte Latin uses SCOIR (pronounced “score”) as its college-planning and predictive-data platform;
college information is made available to families through MyLatin and SCOIR, and freshmen complete
SCOIR registration as part of grade-9 programming.
SCOIR's centerpiece for families is the scattergram: for a given college, it plots a student's GPA against
SAT/ACT results (or a concordance-converted PSAT/NMSQT score when a student has no SAT/ACT yet)
over the school's own history of admits, denials, and waitlists at that college — a data-grounded way to
gauge where a student stands. The high school controls how scattergrams appear: which GPA type is
shown, the range of graduating classes included, and a minimum number of prior acceptances (SCOIR's
default is five) before any data is displayed, and it can turn predictive display on or off.
What isn't published
The school's specific SCOIR configuration — exactly which scattergram settings and predictive features families
can see, and the class-year range shown — is not published publicly. Families can confirm it directly with the
office; its absence from public materials is a transparency limitation, not a sign the tool is unavailable.
Segment sources: Charlotte Latin 2025–26 Upper School Profile and college-counseling pages; historical profiles (2017–18
through 2023–24) for staffing growth; SCOIR product documentation for platform mechanics. Student names are omitted
throughout.

CHARLOTTE LATIN SCHOOL Inside Charlotte Latin College Support
SEGMENT 7 — FIT, RANK & THE WHOLE CLASS
The Honest Questions
No class rank, an explicit fit-over-prestige stance, learning-differences support, and room to
change direction.
The honest questions are about fit and the whole class: how the school keeps high achievers from crowding
one another out, how it supports students who aren't at the top, how it serves students with learning
differences, and whether it defaults to prestige or genuinely optimizes for fit. Charlotte Latin's published
stance leans clearly toward fit and the full class.
Class rank: not reported
Charlotte Latin does not report class rank — a policy stated consistently from the 2017–18 profile through
the current 2025–26 edition. Not ranking is the standard independent-school approach to the crowding
problem: it prevents a school's own strong students from being pitted against one another in a single ordinal
list, so two excellent students aren't separated by a hundredth of a GPA point in a college's eyes.
Fit over prestige, and support beyond the top
The office frames its work around fit rather than a prestige ladder. The Upper School describes the program
as “proactive and student-centered, helping each student identify schools that align with their goals and
passions,” and states plainly: “Urban or pastoral, in state or out of state, Division I or Division III — what
matters most are the dreams students carry, and the colleges that will help them achieve these dreams.”
The breadth of the acceptance list — which spans from open-access and regional universities to the most
selective institutions — is consistent with a whole-class model rather than a top-decile focus.
Students with learning differences
Two offices support students who learn differently. The Learning Resources office (established 1985)
provides teaching, screening, and consultation for documented learning differences, and the newer Office of
Academic Transition and Student Success (ATSS) supports executive functioning, self-advocacy, and
transitions. The college process intersects with these supports.
Accommodation-specific college counseling isn't detailed publicly
While the Learning Resources and ATSS offices are documented, the published materials do not detail
accommodation-specific college-process counseling — for example, disability-disclosure strategy or securing
extended-time documentation for college entrance testing. Families for whom this matters should ask how the
two offices and the college counselors coordinate on it.
When a student changes direction
The fit-first framing and the range of the acceptance list indicate real support for non-traditional directions:
dedicated arts schools (SCAD, Ringling, the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, the School of the
Museum of Fine Arts), international universities (McGill, St Andrews, University College London, Toronto,
Amsterdam, Leiden, Queensland), and the service academies all appear among recent destinations.

CHARLOTTE LATIN SCHOOL Inside Charlotte Latin College Support
SEGMENT 3 — INSTITUTIONAL LEVERAGE
How the School's Name Works for Your Child
The School Profile as a leverage document, a nationally capped Malone designation and a Cum
Laude chapter, and the on-campus channels to colleges.
A School Profile is the document colleges receive alongside every transcript, and Charlotte Latin's is built to
make its students legible to an admissions reader. This segment covers how the profile does that work, the
two credentials the school leads with, and the on-campus channels that connect students to colleges
directly.
How the School Profile contextualizes a student
The profile is written to help an admissions officer interpret a Charlotte Latin transcript correctly. It lays out
the semester system and 21-credit graduation requirements, the benchmark gates for Honors/AP
placement, and — pointedly — the note that the Honors math track is so fast-paced that “many fine math
students are placed in ‘standard’ courses.” That single sentence tells a reader not to penalize a
standard-track placement, which is precisely the leverage a good profile provides: it reframes the transcript
in the school's favor without inflating anything.
The two credentials the school leads with
North Carolina's only Malone Scholars School
Charlotte Latin is the only Malone Scholars School in North Carolina. The Malone Family Foundation caps
the program at 50 independent schools nationally and selects for academic caliber, staff quality,
accommodations for gifted and talented students, strong AP/IB and enrichment programs, financial strength,
a commitment to financial aid, and a diverse population. Being one of a nationally capped group is a
concrete, verifiable marker an admissions reader can weigh.
Cum Laude Society chapter
The school holds a Cum Laude Society chapter — the Edward J. Fox Chapter, chartered in 1976 when the
school was six years old — which signals scholastic honor in the same way a college Phi Beta Kappa
chapter does. The school describes itself as the youngest ever to receive a chapter; that specific claim
appears in the school's own materials and is repeated here as the school's statement rather than as
independently verified fact.
Getting students in front of colleges
• Rep Visits. The school runs a structured college-representative visit program on campus; families and
reps arrange visits through the registrar, and visits are logged so students can meet admissions officers
directly.
• Dean's Panel. The senior year includes a college-admissions panel event.
• Case Studies Mock College Admission + College Fair. Sophomores work through a hands-on
simulation of an admissions committee, paired with a College Fair — demystifying how decisions actually
get made.
• Interview practice is addressed through seminars on effective interview strategy.

The school is a member of NACAC and SACAC and follows their principles of good practice, and is

Schools are sometimes credited with special “relationships” at selective colleges. Charlotte Latin does not

Where Graduates Actually Go
Acceptance vs. matriculation, selectivity by list breadth (not placement rate), a named blended
Top-25, and the athlete slice.
Where do Charlotte Latin graduates actually go? The school publishes a rolling three-year list, and this
segment reads it carefully — separating acceptance from enrollment, measuring the breadth of the list
against current national rankings, and being explicit about the outcome data the school does not publish.
Acceptance list vs. matriculation list
The published document — “Acceptances by the Classes of 2023–25” — is an acceptance list: it names
every college that admitted at least one student across the three-year window. An asterisk marks a college
where at least one student actually matriculated (enrolled) during that period. So the list layers a true
matriculation marker on top of an acceptance list. The current edition names roughly 299 colleges, of which
about 131 carry a matriculation asterisk. Because it is a rolling three-year window, the roster shifts edition
to edition (the prior 2020–22 list, for instance, asterisked a different mix of the most selective schools).

head to Division III and highly selective academic institutions. The school cites a long-run average of roughly

all divisions and activities. Reported here in aggregate only.
Per-class percentages, yield, and persistence are not published

percentages — they describe the list, not a placement rate. These absences are transparency limitations, not
evidence of weak outcomes; families wanting per-class percentages should request them from the office.

| % scoring 4s/5s | — | **NOT PUBLISHED** |

**Exam policy (published, unambiguous):** "Students in AP classes are **required to take the
AP exam**." Placement is gated: "Students must meet certain benchmarks to be placed by faculty
in Honors or AP courses, **with the exception of AP Psychology, AP Economics, AP Environmental
Science, and AP Computer Science Principles**" — i.e. four APs are open-enrollment, the rest
are faculty-gated.

**Full AP roster, 2025–26** (verbatim from the profile's "AP and Advanced Course Options"):

- **English:** AP English Literature
- **Mathematics:** AP Calculus AB, AP Calculus BC, AP Statistics
- **Science:** AP Biology, AP Chemistry, AP Environmental Science*, AP Physics C: Mechanics,
 AP Physics C: Mechanics E/M
- **History/Social Sciences:** AP Economics (includes Macro and Micro)*, AP Comparative
 Government, AP U.S. Government & Politics, AP U.S. History, AP European History, AP Psychology*
- **World Language:** AP French, AP Latin, AP Spanish Language, AP Spanish Literature
- **Innovation/Design:** AP Computer Science A, AP Computer Science Principles,
 **AP Cybersecurity 1: Networking Fundamentals**
- **Performing Arts:** AP Music Theory

(* = course open to students in Grades 11 and 12.)

> **Notable:** AP Cybersecurity is a very new College Board offering; its presence is a
> genuine differentiator worth surfacing.

### AP Scholar ledger (three-year aggregate)

Published on the 2025–26 profile as **"2023-25 ADVANCED PLACEMENT SCHOLARS"**:

| Award | Count (Classes of 2023–25) |
|---|---|
| AP Scholars with Distinction | **193** |
| AP Scholars with Honor | **82** |
| AP Scholars | **143** |
| **Total AP Scholar awards** | **418** (derived sum) |

**Trend across profile editions** — note the College Board **discontinued the AP National
Scholar award** after 2021, which explains its disappearance rather than any decline:

| Profile edition | Window | National Scholars | w/ Distinction | w/ Honor | Scholars |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025–26 | 2023–25 | *(award discontinued)* | 193 | 82 | 143 |
| 2020–21 | 2018–20 | 13 | 48 | 24 | 34 |
| 2019–20 | 2017–19 | 10 | 51 | 19 | 36 |
| 2017–18 | 2017 only | 9 | 36 | 19 | 34 |

> **Interpretation caution / `TO VERIFY`:** the jump from ~48 to 193 Scholars with Distinction
> is very large. Part is real growth (senior class grew from 122 in 2018 to 145 in 2026), but
> the magnitude suggests the counting basis may differ between editions (e.g. cumulative
> awards across all grades vs. graduating-class-only). The school does not define the basis.
> Do not present the 193 as directly comparable to the older 48 without a caveat.

### National Merit ledger

**Current single class — Class of 2026** (school news post, named students):

| Recognition | Count |
|---|---|
| National Merit Semifinalists | **12** |
| Commended Students | **18** |

Named Semifinalists (Class of 2026): Avery Bly, Luca Bravo, June Budzichowski, Emily Cao,
Connor Cruz, Kabir Nawaz, Jackie Rao, Kelsey Sciacca, Isabel Yang, Claire Zhang, Lynn Zhao,
Ryan Zhou.

Named Commended Students (Class of 2026): Max Bai, Ananya Banerjee, Natalie Berman, Hannah
Blackhall, Jolin Cheng, Peter DiSciullo, Eloise Eirich, Samora Elam, Evelyn Haggstrom, Watts
Humphrey, Webb Kiser, Sophia Oh, Divija Rao, Peyton Samii, Wesley Seagraves, Raaj Thakur,
David Vaughn, Angelina Yang.

**Three-year aggregates by profile edition:**

| Window | Semifinalists | Commended | Other |
|---|---|---|---|
| Classes of **2023–25** (current profile) | **20** | **46** | — |
| Classes of 2018–20 | 25 | 34 | 7 National Hispanic Scholars |

**Class of 2024 detail** (from the 2024 Honors and Awards Ceremony): **6 National Merit
Finalists**, **16 Commended Students**, and **1 National Merit Scholar** — Evan Li '24.

> **Discrepancy flagged:** The 2025–26 profile reports **20 Semifinalists across the Classes
> of 2023–25** (a 3-year total). The Class of **2026 alone** produced **12 Semifinalists** —
> more than half the preceding three years combined. Both figures are school-published and
> both are presented above; the apparent surge is real per the sources but is not explained
> by the school.
>
> **Second discrepancy:** the current profile reports Semifinalists and Commended only. It
> **no longer reports Finalists**, which older cycles and the awards ceremony did report.

### College Board National Recognition Program

From the 2024 Honors and Awards Ceremony (the only year located with this detail):

- **National Hispanic and Latino Recognition Program:** Alessandra Martin '25
- **National African American Recognition Program:** Maya Belton '25, Toryn Nichols '24,
 Kenny Ogbata '25, Kwasi Thornhill '24

Counts for other class years are **NOT PUBLISHED**.

### Post-AP / advanced course depth

The profile lists Honors courses that function as post-AP or parallel-advanced work:

- **Mathematics beyond the AP line:** Honors Data Analytics, Honors Intro to Probability &
 Statistics, Honors Math of Social Choice & Management Science. **No multivariable calculus
 or linear algebra is listed** — a genuine ceiling worth noting. The top listed math course
 remains AP Calculus BC.
- **Computer science beyond AP CS A:** **Honors Java Data Structures**, plus AP Cybersecurity 1.
- **Engineering (Honors, non-AP):** Honors Bioengineering, Honors Electrical Engineering.
- **World language beyond AP:** **Honors Greek I–IV** (Greek may only be taken as a *second*
 world language), Honors Latin III/IV, Honors French III/IV, Honors Spanish III/IV, plus both
 AP Spanish Language **and** AP Spanish Literature.
- **Interdisciplinary:** Honors American Studies-History (double-period seminar co-created by
 the History and English departments, taught "at an equivalent level of rigor and depth to
 Advanced Placement curricula" per the 2017–18 profile).
- **Distinctive history seminars:** Honors Food in World History, Honors History of Music
 Seminar, Honors Global Immigration and Migration, Honors Defining Moments: The Civil Rights
 Movement.

**Beyond-campus options:** Older profiles state that electives taken through **NCAIS VisNet**
(the North Carolina Association of Independent Schools virtual network) "are reported on the
CLS transcript but are **not included in the CLS GPA**." The **2025–26 profile does not mention
VisNet or any online/dual-enrollment option** — `TO VERIFY` whether this pathway still exists.

### How the grade is engineered to be trusted

| Mechanism | What Latin publishes |
|---|---|
| GPA scale | **Weighted 4-point scale.** "AP and Honors courses receive **one additional quality point**." (2017–18 profile; the 2025–26 profile omits this statement — see discrepancy below.) |
| Letter/quality-point table | 2017–18 profile published a full table: A+ 4.33 (98–100), A 4.00 (93–97), A− 3.67 (90–92), B+ 3.33 (87–89), B 3.00 (83–86), B− 2.67 (80–82), C+ 2.33 (77–79), C 2.00 (73–76), C− 1.67 (70–72), D+ 1.33 (67–69), D 1.00 (63–66), D− 0.67 (60–62), F 0.00 (<60) |
| Class rank | **"Charlotte Latin School does not report class rank."** (2017–18 profile) |
| Quintile / decile distribution | — **NOT PUBLISHED** in any edition reviewed |
| GPA distribution | — **NOT PUBLISHED** |
| Middle School credit handling | "High school classes completed in Middle School are indicated on the transcript but are **not included in any GPA**." (2025–26 profile) |
| "Most rigorous" course-load norm | Defined structurally, not by label: six courses required per year, four must be academic; **"the recommended and typical course load is five academic courses and one enrichment class."** 21 credits to graduate (English 4, Math 4, Science 3, History 3 incl. World History I & II and U.S. History, World Language 3 in the same language, PE 1 with ½ waivable for athletics). |

**Math-placement transparency (unusually candid, and a real signal to admissions readers):**
the profile explicitly warns colleges not to misread standard-track placement —

> "Our non-honors math curriculum consists of Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II, Advanced
> Functions/Trig (AFT), Precalculus, and Calculus. In general, students may only 'skip' AFT by
> earning an 'A' or 'A−' in Algebra II. Precalculus does not lead directly to AP Calculus; the
> AP Calculus curriculum begins at the end of Honors Precalculus. As our Honors math curriculum
> is unusually rigorous and fast-paced, **many fine math students are placed in 'standard' courses**."

> **Discrepancy flagged — GPA/rank policy disappeared from the current profile.** The
> 2017–18 profile carried an explicit "MARKING SYSTEM" block (weighted 4-point scale, one
> extra quality point for AP/Honors, no class rank) **and** a full letter-grade/quality-point
> table. The **2025–26 profile contains none of this** — no grading scale, no weighting
> statement, no class-rank policy. A college reader of the current profile cannot tell how
> Latin weights or whether it ranks. Both states are documented above; treat the weighting
> and no-rank policy as **`TO VERIFY` for 2025–26** since only the older edition attests them.

> **Publishing-quality defect (worth a tour question).** The published 2025–26 Upper School
> Profile PDF contains an **unedited internal editorial comment left in the live document**,
> immediately after the Academic Program section: *"We'll need to somehow check to make sure
> all these students are still here, yes?"* This is verbatim in the file currently served from
> the school's own resource manager as of 2026-07-26. It is a proofreading lapse in the single
> document every admissions office reads.

### Sources

 2023–25 counts, National Merit 2023–25 counts, graduation requirements, math-placement note,
 Middle School credit policy, editorial-comment defect):

### Four-year 9→12 timeline (verbatim programming)

**Every year (all grades):**
- College information available on **MyLatin and SCOIR**
- Seminars on various college admission topics, such as extracurriculars and summer enrichment
- Periodic informational emails and postings
- Regular appointments and drop-ins
- Informative programs on **Financial Aid for College, Collegiate Athletics, and Arts in College**

**Grade 9 (Freshman):**
- A series of seminars to help students make the most of their Upper School experience
- **SCOIR registration**
- FAQ meeting for parents

**Grade 10 (Sophomore):**
- Seminars on self-discovery — interests and how they translate into college choices
- Individual meetings with counselor on course selection and registration
- **Case Studies Mock College Admission Exercise**, followed by a **College Fair**
- FAQ meeting for parents

**Grade 11 (Junior):**
- Seminars on college visits, interviews, and building an activity résumé
- **Optional summer essay workshops**
- College representative visits
- Individual meetings with counselors on course selection and registration
- **College admissions event featuring a Dean's Panel**
- **Joint meeting** amongst counselor, parent/guardian, and student on the student's
 post-secondary journey
- College Counseling event for parents
- Discussion of **SAT and ACT preparation options and testing timeline**

**Grade 12 (Senior):**
- **College Application Bootcamp**
- Essay review and feedback
- Seminars reviewing the application process
- College rep visits
- **Application assistance, including proofreading each essay and application prior to submission**
- Grade 12 Parent College Night
- **Transition to College Program** for parents

### Application mechanics the office owns

- **Applications:** "review every application prior to submission" (2017–18 profile);
 current page: "Application assistance, including **proofreading each essay and application
 prior to submission**."
- **Essays:** three dedicated essay specialists; senior essay review and feedback; optional
 junior summer essay workshops.
- **Testing:** counselors work with students "on standardized testing timelines"; junior-year
 discussion of SAT/ACT prep options and timeline.
- **Interviews:** "strategies for effective interviews"; the 2017–18 profile specifies
 **mock interviews**.
- **Financial aid:** recurring "Financial Aid for College" program (all-years track).
- **Recruiting/arts tracks:** recurring "Collegiate Athletics" and "Arts in College" programs.
- **Teacher recommendations:** — **NOT PUBLISHED** as an office-owned process. No description
 of how teacher recs are solicited, assigned, or capped.
- **Scholarship search:** — **NOT PUBLISHED** as a named service. No scholarship-search
 platform or dedicated scholarship advising is described on the current page.

### Reach and tools

| Item | Value | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Platform | **SCOIR** (plus the school's own MyLatin portal) | Published, current |
| College rep visits per year | **"nearly 100 college representatives who visit our school each year"** | **Published in the 2017–18 profile only.** The 2025–26 profile and current web page mention rep visits but give **no number** — treat ~100 as `TO VERIFY` / dated |
| Rep-visit scheduling | Older profile: "find us on **Rep Visits**" (contact Sonja Turpin). Current materials name SCOIR | Changed platform — `TO VERIFY` current tool |
| # campus visits made by staff | — | **NOT PUBLISHED** as a count. The 2017–18 profile says counselors "stay current by attending conferences, **visiting colleges**, and speaking extensively with college representatives" — qualitative only |
| Published School Profile | **Yes** — 2025–26 Upper School Profile, linked directly from the College Counseling page | Published |
| CEEB/ACT code | **340663** | Published in the 2019–20 and 2020–21 profiles; **absent from the 2025–26 profile** |
| Office availability | "open throughout the year for appointments and student drop-in visits" | Published |
| Contact | collegecounseling@charlottelatin.org | Published |

> **Discrepancy flagged:** the **CEEB code (340663)** and the dedicated "college reps, contact
> us to arrange a visit" callout both appeared prominently on older profiles and are **gone
> from the 2025–26 edition**. Latin also appears to have **no dedicated "For College
> Representatives" page** — the site navigation lists a "For College Reps" tab on the College
> Counseling page, but the linked pages resolved to Upper School and Campus Map content rather

> **The asterisk convention, stated verbatim on the profile:** "*Indicates college where at least

> **Discrepancy flagged — the "100% to four-year colleges" claim was removed.** All three archived
> editions carried it explicitly: "One hundred percent expect to matriculate at four-year colleges
> or universities" (2017–18, Class of 2018), "100% expect to matriculate at 4-year colleges or
> universities" (2019–20, Class of 2020, and 2020–21, Class of 2021). The **2025–26 profile
> contains no four-year-college percentage at all.** Whether this reflects a policy change, a
> change in the outcome, or simply a redesign is **not explained by the school**. Do not carry the
> 100% figure forward to the current class — it is `TO VERIFY` and attaches to Classes of 2018–21.

### Selectivity buckets — Ivy League (scored against the 2026 U.S. News tables)

**5 of 8 Ivies appear on the 2023–25 list, all 5 with matriculation asterisks:**

| Harvard University | Yes | **Yes** (*) |

| **Princeton University** | **ABSENT** | — |
| **University of Pennsylvania** | **ABSENT** | — |

> appear anywhere on the 300-institution list — meaning **no acceptance was reported** to any of
> the three across the Classes of 2023–25. Verified by direct string search of the extracted PDF
> text, including checks for "Princeton", "Columbia", "Pennsylvania" and "Penn". A separate fetch
> of the school's own web Acceptances page returned a summary that *asserted* Princeton was
> present; that assertion is **contradicted by the authoritative PDF** and is treated as an error

**MIT*** (both with matriculation asterisks), **Stanford University** and **University of
Chicago** (both **accepted only, no matriculation asterisk**). Also absent from the whole list:

|---|---|---|

> school-published figures**. They were produced by matching the parsed 300-row list against 2026
> U.S. News rank tables. U.S. News publishes heavy **ties** at the 70–75 boundary and gates the
> full ordered table behind its site, so the exact membership of ranks ~55–75 could not be
> independently confirmed from a free source during this pass. Treat both as **±3** and as
> approximate. The Ivy and Power Four counts, by contrast, are **exact** — those memberships are
> fixed and unambiguous.

> **The Power Four finding is the striking one.** Of the 64 Power Four institutions, **63 appear
> on the list** — every ACC school (19/19), every SEC school (16/16), every Big 12 school (12/12),

> clearest quantitative evidence of the list's sheer breadth.

CHARLOTTE LATIN SCHOOL Inside Charlotte Latin College Support
SEGMENT 5 — STANDING OUT
Cultivating a Distinct “Hook”
Seminar-based support for building a coherent profile, and process-level help for recruited athletes
and arts applicants.
“Standing out” is about helping a student build a distinct, non-generic profile — a “hook” or “spike” — and
supporting the specialized pathways of recruited athletes and arts applicants at the process level. Charlotte
Latin approaches this mainly through structured seminars rather than a single branded program.
Developing a distinct profile
The counseling calendar builds toward differentiation deliberately: sophomore-year self-discovery seminars
help students translate genuine interests into college direction, and later seminars focus on extracurriculars,
summer enrichment, and building an activity résumé that reads as coherent rather than scattered. The aim
is to help a student articulate what makes them distinctive, not to manufacture a persona.
Recruited athletes and arts applicants
• Collegiate Athletics seminar. A dedicated session addresses the recruiting process for student-athletes
— at the college-support level (timelines, communication, eligibility awareness), distinct from on-field
coaching.
• Arts in College seminar. A parallel session addresses portfolio development and audition pathways for
students pursuing college arts programs.
What “standing out” support is — and isn't
These are process supports: they help a student navigate the recruiting or portfolio pathway and shape a
coherent profile. They are not a guarantee of a “spike,” and the school does not publish a distinct, branded
“hook-building” methodology. Athletic families targeting the most competitive programs should confirm what
recruiting-timeline and highlight-film support the office provides versus what team coaches handle. (Deep athletic
recruiting data lives outside this college-support review.)

College Counseling at Charlotte Latin School: A Program
Review (2025–26)
TL;DR
Charlotte Latin's College Counseling Office is a well-sta"ed, stable operation — four
full-time counselors led by longtime director Jody Jennings, plus a registrar, an
administrative assistant, and three named essay specialists — that assigns each
student a counselor and uses SCOIR (not Naviance) for scattergrams and predictive
data; the office grew from three counselors in 2017–18 to four by 2019.
The school publishes a fresh 2025–26 Upper School Profile and an updated
"Acceptances by the Classes of 2023-25" list; strongest recent outcomes include the
Class of 2026's 12 National Merit Semifinalists and 18 Commended Students, a
2023–25 aggregate of 193 AP Scholars with Distinction, and asterisked
(matriculation) Ivy results at Brown, Cornell, Dartmouth, Harvard, and Yale.
Multiple quantitative items families often want — AP exam pass rates, school-
published SAT/ACT ranges, per-class selective-tier percentages, college-specific
yield, and post-enrollment persistence — are NOT published by the school; these are
transparency gaps, not evidence of weakness.
Key Findings
1. Counseling engine is deep and stable. The published 2025–26 team is four full-time
counselors (Jody Jennings, Director; Haley Cripps, Lucy Smith, Alex Segura, Associate
Directors), a registrar (Sonja Turpin), an administrative assistant (Stacey Rommich), and
three essay specialists (Andrea Powell, Marty Minchin, Mary Beth Foster '99). The office
has grown from three counselors in 2017–18 to four since roughly 2019, and the four-
counselor core has been consistent across at least the 2022–23, 2023–24, and 2025–26
profiles. The platform is SCOIR. charlottelatin Charlottelatin

AP/Honors, and the school does not report class rank. charlottelatin Charlottelatin

Scholars School status and the Cum Laude Society chapter (chartered 1976). Rep Visits, the
